newsitem.title: USA: Hubble service crew prepares to return home.
newsitem.headline: Hubble service crew prepares to return home.

text.p: NASA's Hubble tune-up crew hung up their spacesuits on Thursday and prepared for a rare nighttime landing at the Kennedy Space Centre.
The seven-man crew, who successfully refurbished the Hubble Space Telescope during five outings into space, packed away their spacewalking gear and checked out shuttle Discovery's landing systems.

Forecasters were predicting generally favourable weather for the planned touchdown at 1:49 a.m. EST (0649 GMT) on Friday. The only concern was over a chance of showers within 35 miles (56 km) of the runway.
"The weather for the Cape tomorrow is looking fairly good," mission control's Kevin Kregel told the shuttle crew. "We think we have a good chance of getting into Kennedy."
Conditions at the Florida spaceport were forecast to deteriorate on Saturday and NASA dispatched recovery crews to the back-up landing strip in California, where the weather was expected to be fine.

The shuttle, running low on electrical power and other supplies, had to be home by Sunday, flight director Wayne Hale told a news conference on Thursday. He expected the mission would end on one coast or the other by Saturday.
In preparation for Friday's homecoming, mission commander Ken Bowersox and copilot Scott Horowitz test-fired Discovery's manoeuvring jets and powered up the hydraulic system.

The landing would be only the ninth in the shuttle programme to take place in darkness. But it will be aided by the recent installation of 52 Halogen lights down the centre of the 15,000-foot (4,572 metre) -long runway. Shuttle commanders requested the modification to help them keep the gliding shuttle lined up for a perfect touchdown.
NASA officials said they expected nighttime and low-light dawn landings to become more commonplace.

As their 10-day mission drew to a close, the astronauts took in the sights from 385 miles (620 km) up -- a record for a civilian shuttle mission. Looking down at the nighttime portion of Earth they could see city lights stretching out along the U.S. East Coast from Key West to north of New York.
"The view from up here is absolutely fantastic," crew member Joe Tanner said. "You could see almost the entire United States in one window."
In the opposite direction, Comet Hale-Bopp graced the night sky above Discovery. Astronomers have high hopes for the comet, which is already visible to the naked eye.

"It appears to have two tails, one tail about three times longer than the other," astronaut Steve Hawely, a former astronomer, said. "Really a tremendous sight. This is a good place to observe it, high above the atmosphere."

Discovery blasted off from the Kennedy Space Centre before dawn on Feb. 11. The astronauts captured the Hubble Space Telescope two days later and made $350 million worth of upgrades before releasing it again early on Wednesday.
